extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, educators, and legal researchers interested in First Amendment and school law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the legal standards and practical criteria U.S. courts use to evaluate and regulate student speech in public schools (e.g., Tinker, Fraser, Hazelwood, Morse, Mahanoy). Includes factors for on-campus and off-campus, online speech, and school‑sponsored expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tinker test — substantial disruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech may be regulated if it would 'materially and substantially interfere with the requirements of appropriate discipline in the operation of the school' (the Tinker substantial disruption test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core example: students wearing black armbands protesting the Vietnam War was not disruptive and thus protected. Courts ask whether the student's speech poses a substantial threat of disruption to classwork or discipline; if so, school regulation is permissible. Applied to both in‑school and, in some cases, off‑campus speech depending on nexus and foreseeability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraser standard — vulgar/sexually offensive speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools may discipline student speech that is vulgar, lewd, indecent, or plainly offensive even if it is not obscene; balance students' speech rights against the school's interest in teaching civility and socially appropriate behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a student's sexually suggestive remarks at a school assembly could be punished under Fraser. The test emphasizes the school's pedagogical interest in inculcating habits of civility and may be applied even when Tinker disruption is not shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazelwood standard — school‑sponsored/curricular speech
rubrics_metrics.description: School authorities may exercise editorial control over student speech that is part of school‑sponsored or curricular activities so long as their actions are reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: censoring articles in a school newspaper produced as part of a journalism curriculum. The key is whether the speech is school‑sponsored/part of the educational mission and whether the censorship reasonably relates to pedagogical objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morse rule — speech advocating illegal drug use at school events
rubrics_metrics.description: A school may restrict student speech at a school‑sanctioned event when the speech is reasonably viewed as promoting illegal drug use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a banner at a school event reading 'BONG HiTS 4 JESUS' was permissibly suppressed. Morse blends Fraser and Hazelwood principles and focuses on messages that contradict the school's policy/mission (e.g., drug prevention) at school‑sanctioned activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off‑campus speech and Mahanoy considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Tinker may apply to off‑campus student speech that is disruptive to the school, but the Supreme Court has left unresolved many boundaries; off‑campus speech generally receives greater protection though schools may regulate disruptive off‑campus speech in some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mahanoy (B.L.) held the school interests under Tinker were insufficient to overcome First Amendment rights for a profane off‑campus Snapchat post, but left open when regulation of off‑campus speech is permissible for lower courts. Important factors: nexus to school, disruption, and whether speech was directed at the school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, place, and manner reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech regulations may be upheld if they are reasonable limits on the time, place, and manner of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right of free speech is not absolute; courts routinely uphold reasonable T/P/M restrictions. In the school context reasonableness is evaluated with attention to context and the school's educational mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and maturity of students as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The age and maturity of the student body are important considerations when courts assess the reasonableness of speech regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Younger students may be subject to broader regulation; courts have repeatedly noted that maturity affects how speech is evaluated in schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewpoint discrimination prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrimination against speech because of its message or viewpoint is presumed unconstitutional; viewpoint‑specific restrictions are especially disfavored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rosenberger and Tinker principles emphasize that denying speech funding or access solely because of its message (e.g., religious viewpoint) is unconstitutional. Schools must avoid regulating speech based on viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensiveness test — 'plainly offensive' sexual content
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts evaluate whether speech is 'plainly offensive' in sexual content or implication (distinct from merely expressing offensive ideas), which can justify regulation under Fraser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saxe and related authorities limit offensiveness analysis to sexual/vulgar content rather than unpopular beliefs; context (assembly vs private speech) matters. Offensiveness often does not apply to off‑campus speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impairing the school's educational mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that, if allowed as part of a school activity or function, would be contrary to the basic educational mission of the school may be regulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazelwood applied this to curricular student media on issues like divorce or teenage pregnancy; Morse applied it to banners promoting drug use. The standard looks to legitimate pedagogical concerns and supportive learning environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure speech factor (symbols/actions vs. curricular activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the activity is 'pure speech' (symbols or actions sufficiently related to expression of ideas) affects First Amendment analysis and potential protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure speech (including symbolic acts) may enjoy broader protection; courts analyze whether the activity is expressive and the degree it is related to protected expression versus school functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus of protected speech activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The focus or nature of the protected activity (pure speech, curricular/extra‑curricular, online, symbolic) affects whether and how regulation is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether speech is school‑connected (curricular, school‑sponsored) or personal/off‑campus speech and tailor analysis accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location/nexus — on‑campus vs off‑campus and use of school resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The geographic and functional connection of the speech to the school (on school property, at school time, using school resources, or directed at the school) matters for jurisdiction to regulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases differentiate speech made on campus or during school activities (more regulable) from speech prepared and distributed off campus without school involvement (less regulable). Use of school resources or distribution on campus can bring speech under school authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreseeability and directedness toward the school
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech originating off campus but intentionally directed at the school or foreseeably reaching the school community can be treated as on‑campus speech for regulatory purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge concurrences/dissents discuss applying Tinker to off‑campus emails or posts that are aimed at faculty/students; courts evaluate intent to reach the school and reasonable foreseeability of on‑campus impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance of school sponsorship or endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: When student speech reasonably appears to be sponsored, endorsed, or approved by the school, the school has greater authority to regulate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazelwood and subsequent cases emphasize that speech seeming school‑endorsed (e.g., at a school function or carrying school imprimatur) may be regulated to avoid implied endorsement or disruption of the educational mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threats and true threats (violence‑related speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that constitutes a true threat or communicates a credible plan of violence is not protected and may be punished to prevent foreseeable harm or disruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a student posting or sharing threats of a school shooting or imagery suggesting intent to kill a teacher has been treated as sufficient to allow discipline under disruption/public safety doctrines (Wisniewski, LaVine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Online/offline harassment and bullying causing disruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Online speech (blogs, social media, websites) that harasses, targets, or ridicules students or staff and causes substantial disruption or violates anti‑bullying policies can be regulated by schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuits have varied, but discipline has been upheld where online content produced off campus was directed at the school community and produced substantial disruption or harm to victims (e.g., MySpace profile, derogatory websites). Courts consider content, audience, reach, and impact on school environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of content‑based analyses vs. content‑neutral restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a regulation is content‑based (targeting particular subject matter or viewpoint) or content‑neutral affects constitutional scrutiny and permissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content/viewpoint‑based restrictions are disfavored and can trigger stricter review; neutral rules about time/place/manner or discipline for conduct/threats may be easier for schools to justify.
